14770:
A sneer is an expression — on someone's face, in their voice, or in their words — that communicates contempt and superiority. When someone sneers, they are essentially saying, without necessarily using words: "You are beneath me. This is pathetic. I have no respect for this."

It is the expression of someone who is looking down on another person or thing.
What It Looks Like on a Face

The most classic form of a sneer is a facial expression. Picture this:

  • The upper lip curls upward, usually more on one side than the other — like a twisted, cold half-smile
  • The nostrils may flare slightly
  • The eyes are often cold, narrowed, or dismissive

It is not a warm smile. It is not an angry scowl. It sits somewhere in between — a controlled, almost lazy expression that says the person doesn't even think you're worth getting angry at. They simply think you are inferior, ridiculous, or worthless.

A bully looking at a smaller, weaker child with that cold, curled-lip look? That is a sneer.

The engine that drives a sneer is contempt — which means a deep feeling that someone or something is worthless, weak, or beneath one's dignity. Contempt is actually a more powerful and cutting emotion than anger. Anger says "you matter enough to upset me." Contempt says "you don't even matter enough to upset me."

A sneer is the visible face of contempt. It says:

  • "I pity you, but not in a kind way."
  • "You are laughable."
  • "This is beneath me."

This is why a sneer is so often associated with arrogance, snobbery, and cruelty.

A sneer doesn't have to be only a facial expression. It can also be a remark or comment — something someone says in a tone dripping with mockery and contempt. This verbal sneer is not a direct insult necessarily, but the attitude embedded in it is unmistakably dismissive and belittling.

Example: If someone shows you a painting they made with great pride, and you say flatly — "Oh. How... quaint." — with a curl of disdain in your voice, that response is a sneer. You haven't screamed an insult. But you've made it crystal clear that you think the painting (and possibly the person) is laughably inferior.

Understanding what a sneer is not will sharpen your understanding of what it is.

Sneer vs. Smirk: A smirk is a self-satisfied, smug little smile — it's mostly about the person feeling pleased with themselves. A sneer is directed outward, at someone else, with contempt. A smirk says "I'm clever." A sneer says "You're pathetic."

Sneer vs. Scowl: A scowl is driven by anger or disapproval — it's heavy, furrowed, intense. A sneer is more cold and superior. A scowl says "I am upset." A sneer says "I am above you." The sneer is actually more insulting precisely because it's so calm — the person can't even be bothered to get truly angry at you.

Sneer vs. Grimace: A grimace is a reaction to pain, discomfort, or disgust — it's usually involuntary. A sneer is deliberate and directed at someone with intent to belittle.

• The wealthy guest gave a sneer at the small, modest house, as if he found the whole place embarrassing.
  • "Is that really what you're wearing?" she said with a sneer that made him feel two inches tall.
  • The older students greeted the newcomer's idea with sneers and quiet laughter.
  • Despite his sneers, she continued speaking confidently.
The Feeling of Receiving a Sneer

This is important to understand the word fully: being on the receiving end of a sneer is a distinctly unpleasant experience. It stings more than outright shouting sometimes, because the sneer communicates that the other person doesn't even take you seriously enough to argue with. It is designed — consciously or not — to make you feel small, foolish, and inferior.

This is why sneers are so commonly associated with bullies, villains, snobs, and condescending authority figures in literature and film. The sneer is the calling card of someone who believes they are superior and wants you to feel it.

A sneer is a cold, contemptuous expression — in the face, voice, or words — that communicates superiority and disrespect. It is the visible and audible shape of looking down on someone. It is more cutting than anger because it carries the message that the other person is not even worth your full emotional energy — only your contempt.
14771:
To sneer means to show contempt toward someone or something — to make it obvious that you think they are stupid, worthless, inferior, or not worthy of your respect.

The key feeling locked inside this word is contempt — that cold, dismissive sense of "you are beneath me." Not just dislike. Not just disagreement. But a feeling that something or someone is pathetically below your standard, and you want to make that feeling visible.

Sneering happens in two closely related ways, and both often happen together:

1. With Your Face

You make a particular expression — usually by curling or twisting one side of your upper lip upward. It is not a smile. It is a twisted, mocking, cold expression that communicates "I find you ridiculous." Think of a bully looking at someone's lunch and pulling that half-smile, half-grimace face. That is a sneer.

2. With Your Words

You say something in a tone that drips with mockery and dismissiveness. The way you say it — cold, cutting, superior — is what makes it a sneer. The words themselves might be ordinary, but the sneering tone makes them feel like a slap.

"Oh, so you wrote a little poem," he sneered.

The quote above shows how a sneer can be expressed through speech — the tone here is sarcastic and belittling.

What separates "sneer" from simply being rude or critical is the attitude of superiority behind it. When someone sneers, they are not just expressing displeasure — they are signaling:

  • "I am above you."
  • "You and your efforts are laughable."
  • "This doesn't even deserve my serious attention."

It is contempt performed — deliberately shown so that the other person feels small.

Sneer is most commonly used in two patterns:

Pattern 1: sneer + at + someone/something
This is the most natural and common structure.

  • She sneered at his cheap suit.
  • The critics sneered at the young artist's first exhibition.
  • He sneered at the idea of asking for help.

Pattern 2: sneer + (something said in quotes)
Here, "sneer" replaces a word like "say" or "reply" to show how someone spoke.

  • "You actually think you can beat me?" she sneered.
  • "How impressive," he sneered, not meaning it at all.

Situation 1:
A talented chef watches a beginner cook a simple dish. Instead of offering advice, she curls her lip and says, "You call that cooking?" — She is sneering. She feels superior and is showing it openly.

Situation 2:
A wealthy person sees someone wearing budget clothing and gives them a slow, mocking look up and down — that facial expression is a sneer. No words needed.

Situation 3:
A politician sneers at his opponent's ideas in a debate — dismissing them not with logical arguments, but with mocking laughter and a tone that says "this is too silly to even take seriously."
What Makes "Sneer" Different from Similar Words

These words are close cousins, but they are not identical:

Scoff — Very similar, but scoffing tends to be more about dismissing something with a sharp, vocal sound or laugh (like a quick, contemptuous "Ha!"). Sneering is more sustained and can be purely facial.

Mock — To mock is to imitate or make fun of someone, often in an exaggerated, theatrical way. Sneering is more subtle and internal — it is contempt shown on the face or in tone, not necessarily a full-blown imitation.

Jeer — Jeering is louder and more aggressive, often done in groups (think a crowd jeering at a player). Sneering is quieter and more personal — even one raised eyebrow can be a sneer.

Smirk — A smirk is a self-satisfied, sly little smile, often suggesting "I know something you don't" or "I told you so." A sneer is uglier and more openly contemptuous.

Look down on — This is the broad attitude; sneering is how that attitude shows up on the face or in speech.
The Register: Who Uses This Word and When?

"Sneer" is a standard English word used in both formal writing (novels, essays, journalism) and everyday speech. It appears very often in literature and news to describe how characters or public figures respond to others with contempt. It carries a slightly negative connotation — the person sneering is almost never the hero of the moment. Sneering is generally seen as an ugly, arrogant behavior.
To sneer is to show — through your face, your tone, or your words — that you find someone or something contemptibly beneath you, making your sense of superiority visible in a cold, mocking way.
14772: When you snicker, you laugh in a quiet, partly suppressed way — usually at someone or something, in a mocking or disrespectful manner. It's the laugh you try to hold back but can't quite kill. It slips out quietly, often through your nose or with your lips barely parted.

A snicker is not a full, open, honest laugh. It's secretive. It's the kind of laugh that happens when someone trips and falls, and you know you shouldn't laugh, but a little "heh heh" escapes anyway. It's small, stifled, and often sneaky.

Think of it physically: your shoulders might shake slightly, you might cover your mouth, and the sound is more of a breathy, nasal "heh-heh-heh" than a bright "ha-ha-ha."

What makes "snicker" distinct is its attitude. Almost always, it carries a sharp little edge of:

  • Mockery — laughing at someone, not with them
  • Superiority — finding someone or something beneath you, amusing in a condescending way
  • Secretiveness — often done behind someone's back, or just quietly enough that they might not notice

This is not warm laughter. It's not the laugh of a friend enjoying a joke together with you. It's the laugh of people huddled together finding someone else ridiculous.
How it feels to be snickered at

If someone snickers at you, it stings. You feel mocked. You feel small. The person snickering isn't confronting you openly — they're being sly about it. That sneakiness is part of what makes it unkind.
How it compares to similar words

Laugh is the neutral, general word. It carries no particular attitude on its own.

Giggle is a light, often innocent laugh — usually associated with nervousness, silliness, or something genuinely funny. A child giggling is cute. A snicker never really feels cute.

Chuckle is a soft, warm, mild laugh — the kind a kind grandfather gives at a gentle joke. It's good-natured.

Snicker sits in its own corner: suppressed + mocking. That combination is what makes it unique. If you remember nothing else, remember this: a snicker is a laugh you're trying to hide, and there's usually someone being looked down upon.

Occasionally, "snicker" is used for a suppressed laugh that isn't particularly cruel — for example, when something is genuinely funny but you're in a situation where laughing openly would be inappropriate (a serious meeting, a quiet library, a solemn ceremony). In those cases, the suppression is out of social propriety, not malice.

But even then, there's almost always a hint of irreverence or private amusement at something that "shouldn't" be funny. The word almost never feels entirely warm and innocent.

• The students snickered when the professor accidentally called the country by its old name.
    → They found it funny and mocking; they tried not to laugh openly, but couldn't help it.
  • She could hear them snickering behind her back as she walked away.
    → They were laughing at her quietly and secretly, in a way she wasn't meant to see clearly.
  • He snickered at the irony — the man who fired half the team had just been fired himself.
    → Here it's less cruel but still a private, knowing, slightly sharp little laugh.
  • Don't snicker — she's trying her best.
    → A reprimand; someone is laughing quietly in a dismissive or unkind way.
To snicker is to let out a small, suppressed, quietly mocking laugh — the kind that escapes when you find someone or something faintly ridiculous, and you're trying (not very hard) to hide it.
14773:
When something is snide, it is indirectly cruel or mocking. A snide remark doesn't attack you openly and honestly — it stings you in a sneaky, sly way. It hides its meanness behind a thin cover of normality, so that on the surface it almost sounds fine, but underneath it carries contempt, mockery, or disrespect.

Think of it this way: if someone punches you in the face, that is direct and obvious. But if someone gives you a "friendly" pat on the back that is just a little too hard and a little too deliberate — that is more like being snide. The hostility is real, but it is wrapped up.

A snide remark has three qualities working together:

1. It is indirect. The criticism or mockery is not stated outright. It is implied, suggested, or smuggled in through tone, word choice, or sarcasm.

2. It is demeaning. The person making it looks down on you. There is a sense of superiority in it — the speaker feels clever, or better than you, and wants you to feel small.

3. It is deliberate. A snide person knows exactly what they are doing. They are not accidentally being rude. They are choosing to be subtle about it, often so they can deny it later or simply enjoy the feeling of getting away with it.

Let's say your friend has been trying to learn to cook, and they finally make a decent meal.

  • Honest praise: "This is really good! You've improved a lot."
  • Direct insult: "Your cooking was terrible before."
  • Snide remark: "Wow, I can actually eat this one."

That last one is snide. Notice how it doesn't say anything directly insulting — but it clearly implies that your previous cooking was bad, said with a kind of smug amusement. It stings, but the speaker can shrug and say, "What? It was a compliment!"

More examples:

  • A colleague who always wanted your promotion sees you struggling with a task and says: "Oh, don't worry — not everyone is cut out for this role." → Snide. It sounds almost sympathetic, but it's actually a quiet put-down.
  • Someone looks at your new haircut and says, with a small smirk: "Well, that's... a choice." → Snide. They haven't said it's bad, but the tone, the pause, and the word "choice" communicate that they think it looks terrible.
  • A person says "Must be nice to have so much free time" to someone they secretly resent. → Snide. Phrased almost as a casual observation, but loaded with quiet resentment and judgment.

Understanding what snide is not will sharpen the picture:

  • Not the same as just "rude." Rude is direct and obvious. "Your idea is stupid" is rude. Snide is more covert and slippery.
  • Not the same as honest criticism. Honest criticism is straightforward and usually well-intentioned. Snide remarks are not meant to help you — they are meant to diminish you.
  • Not the same as a joke. A joke between friends can tease without malice. A snide remark has an edge of real contempt in it.
  • Not always loud. Snide is often quiet, even polite-sounding. The danger is in what is implied, not what is stated.

When someone is snide toward you, you often feel a specific kind of confusion at first — "Wait, was that an insult?" — followed by the slow, uncomfortable realization that yes, it was. You feel mocked but cannot easily confront it, because the other person has left themselves an escape route. This is part of what makes snide behaviour particularly unpleasant: it is hard to challenge, and it makes you feel like you are overreacting if you call it out.

The person being snide, on the other hand, often has a self-satisfied, smug quality — as though they have just been very clever.

The word "snide" can describe:

  • A remark or comment — "a snide remark" (most common use)
  • A tone or manner — "he said it in a snide tone"
  • A look or expression — "a snide little smile"
  • A person — "she can be so snide" (meaning they often speak or behave this way)
  • Humour — "snide humour" (comedy that mocks others in this sly, superior way)

These words are related and will help you understand the territory around "snide":

  • Cutting — Sharp and hurtful (but often more direct than snide)
  • Sarcastic — Saying the opposite of what you mean, mockingly
  • Condescending — Talking down to someone, treating them as inferior
  • Disparaging — Expressing low regard or disrespect for someone
  • Sneering — Showing contempt, often through expression or tone

Of these, snide is unique because it combines slyness with contempt — it is not just about what is said, but how deliberately it is hidden.

Snide = indirectly and slyly disrespectful — a remark or attitude that mocks or demeans someone in a subtle, covert way, rather than honestly and directly.

If you ever feel insulted but cannot quite put your finger on how, and you sense the other person did it on purpose and is enjoying it — that is almost certainly something snide.
14774:
To sniffle means to repeatedly draw air up through your nose in small, short, quiet bursts — making a soft, slightly wet sound each time. It is not one deliberate sniff; it is a series of small, involuntary sniffs happening one after another because your nose keeps producing fluid that you cannot (or do not want to) blow out.

Think of it this way: when your nose is running, instead of reaching for a tissue, your body naturally tries to pull that fluid back up. That repeated, gentle pulling-in action — with its soft little sound — is sniffling.
When and why people sniffle

There are two main situations:

1. When you are sick or have a cold.
Your nose produces a lot of mucus, and it keeps running. You sniffle to pull it back up again and again throughout the day. This is purely physical — your body doing what it can to manage a runny nose.

2. When you are crying, sad, or trying not to cry.
Tears do not only come out of your eyes — they also drain inward through tiny passages into your nose. This is why your nose runs when you cry. As a result, people sniffle during or after crying. Even when someone is trying to hold back tears and not fully crying, the nose still reacts, and so they sniffle. This is why sniffling is strongly associated with sadness and emotional vulnerability.
What it looks, sounds, and feels like

• The sound is soft, quiet, and slightly wet — not dramatic, not loud.
  • It is repetitive. One sniffle leads to another because the cause (the runny nose) does not go away immediately.
  • The body's movement is small — just the nose and the breath, not the whole body.
  • It conveys restraint. It is what happens when you are containing an emotion or illness, not fully releasing it.
The feeling and tone the word carries

"Sniffle" is not a neutral word. It has a tender, slightly vulnerable quality to it. When a writer says a character sniffled, you immediately picture someone delicate, sad, or unwell — a sick child in bed, someone who just got bad news, a person trying hard not to cry in public, or someone quietly weeping alone.

It is a word that creates sympathy. It makes the person seem human and a little helpless in that moment.
How it is used in sentences

• She sniffled quietly as she read his message.
  • He had been sniffling all day because of his cold.
  • The child sniffled and wiped her eyes with her sleeve.
  • "I'm fine," she said, though she kept sniffling.
  • He sniffled throughout the entire film.
  • Stop sniffling and just blow your nose!

Notice how in all of these, the sniffling is ongoing or repeated — not a single moment, but something that continues for a while.
The different grammatical forms

• sniffle — the base form (I always sniffle when I cry.)
  • sniffles / sniffling — ongoing action (She is sniffling. He sniffles every time he has a cold.)
  • sniffled — past tense (He sniffled as he walked away.)
How "sniffle" differs from similar words
Sniff vs. sniffle

A sniff is a single, deliberate, conscious action — you sniff a flower, you sniff something to check if it smells bad. A sniffle is involuntary, soft, and repeated — you do not choose to sniffle, it just happens because your nose is reacting to something.
Sniffle vs. sob
A sob is much more intense — it involves a loud, shaky breath, a heaving chest, and obvious distress. A sniffle is quiet and restrained. If sobbing is a storm, sniffling is a light drizzle.
Sniffle vs. cry/weep

Crying or weeping refers to the full emotional act — tears, sounds, the whole experience. Sniffling is something that happens around crying: before it starts, after it ends, or when someone is trying to stop it. You can sniffle without crying at all — for instance, just from a cold.
Sniffle vs. blow your nose

These are opposite actions. Blowing your nose pushes air outward to clear it. Sniffling pulls air inward, drawing the fluid back up. Sniffling does not actually solve the problem — it just temporarily keeps it at bay, which is part of why it seems a bit helpless.
A quick summary

To sniffle is to make repeated, soft, quiet nasal sounds by drawing air up through the nose — typically when you have a cold or when you are emotional. It is quiet, involuntary, and continuous. The word carries a tone of vulnerability and restraint, and it is one of the most human, relatable sounds there is.
14775:
To snip means to cut something using scissors (or a similar sharp tool like shears or garden clippers) with a short, quick, single cutting motion. The cut is small and precise — not a long sweep, not a heavy chop, just a brief, clean snick of the blades.

That's the heart of it: small + quick + scissors = snip.
What Makes Snipping Different from Just "Cutting"

Not every cut is a snip. The word carries specific qualities that you must understand:

1. The tool matters.
You almost always snip with scissors or scissor-like tools — not a knife, not an axe, not your hands. The word strongly implies two blades coming together.

2. The cut is small.
You snip a thread, not a log. You snip a little off the end, not through something thick and large. The action is delicate and controlled.

3. The motion is brief.
One quick, decisive closing of the blades. It's not a prolonged sawing or slicing. Even if you do it many times in a row, each individual snip is a short, sharp motion.

4. Precision is implied.
When you snip something, you're doing it carefully and intentionally. It suggests neatness and care — the opposite of hacking or tearing.
How Snip Relates to Similar Words

It helps to see how "snip" sits among words with related meanings:

  • Cut is the broad, general word. Any severing action is a "cut." Snip is a specific type of cut — small, quick, with scissors.
  • Trim means to cut away untidy or excess parts to make something neat (trim your beard, trim the edges of a photo). Snip can be part of trimming, but trimming is the goal while snipping is the action.
  • Clip is very close to snip. You clip a coupon, clip your nails, clip a hedge. The difference is subtle: clip often suggests cutting along a surface or cutting to neaten/shorten, while snip emphasizes a single, quick cutting action to separate a small piece cleanly. In practice, the two overlap a lot, and native speakers sometimes use them interchangeably in casual contexts.
  • Shear is for large-scale cutting, like cutting wool off sheep or cutting metal with heavy tools.
  • Chop is forceful, usually done with a heavy blade (chop wood, chop vegetables). Snip is gentle and precise by comparison.

The word naturally pairs with small, cuttable things:

  • Thread or string — a tailor snips the loose threads after sewing
  • Hair — a hairdresser snips a few strands to even out a haircut
  • Fabric — snip a small notch into the edge before folding it
  • Plant stems, flowers, herbs — a gardener snips a rose from its stem; a cook snips fresh chives over a dish
  • Tags and labels — snip the price tag off a new shirt
  • Coupons — snip a discount coupon out of a newspaper
  • Ribbon — snip the ribbon to open a package or finish a gift
  • Wire — snip a thin wire with wire cutters
  • Sutures (in medicine) — a doctor snips stitches to remove them

You'll often see "snip" combined with small words that give it a slightly different direction:

Snip off — to remove something by cutting it away from the main body.
"She snipped off the dead flower so the plant could grow better."
"He snipped off the corner of the envelope to open it."

Snip out — to cut something out from within a larger piece.
"She snipped out the recipe from the magazine."

Snip away — to keep snipping repeatedly, cutting bit by bit.
"The hairdresser snipped away at the split ends."
"He snipped away at the hedge until it was perfectly shaped."

Here are examples that show the word in action across different situations:

  • "She snipped the thread and held up the finished seam." — sewing
  • "The barber snipped a little more off the sides." — haircut
  • "Snip the ends off the green beans before cooking them." — cooking
  • "He snipped a few sprigs of rosemary from the garden." — gardening
  • "She snipped the coupon carefully so the barcode wouldn't be damaged." — couponing
  • "The doctor snipped the sutures and the wound was finally healed." — medicine
  • "He snipped the ribbon and the ceremony was officially over." — formal event
  • "Just snip off that loose thread and your shirt will look perfect." — everyday use

One more thing worth noting: "snip" carries a slightly light, almost satisfying feel to it. It's not violent or heavy. When you snip something, you're in control. You're being careful, methodical, precise. The word almost sounds like what it describes — that crisp little snip of scissor blades. This is part of why it feels different from "cut" or "chop," which are more neutral or forceful.

To snip is to make a small, quick, clean cut using scissors or a similar tool. It is precise, controlled, and brief. You snip small things — thread, hair, herb stems, tags, coupons — to separate them or remove a small portion. The action is delicate, not aggressive. That combination of scissors + small + quick + precise is what makes something a snip and not just a cut.
14776: To snipe means to attack from a hidden or safe position, with precision, in a way that is hard for the target to defend against or respond to. That idea — hidden, precise, one-sided — runs through every use of this word.

To snipe originally means to shoot at a target from a concealed, distant position, usually with a high-accuracy rifle. The person doing this is called a sniper.

The key elements are:

  • Distance — the shooter is far away.
  • Concealment — the shooter is hidden; the target cannot easily see them.
  • Precision — it is a careful, aimed shot, not random firing.
  • Vulnerability — the target has little warning and little chance to fight back.

"Enemy soldiers were sniped at from rooftops as they moved through the street."

Because of those same qualities — hidden, one-sided, targeted — to snipe also means to make sharp, critical, or mean remarks about someone, especially in a petty or constant way.

It carries a specific flavor: the person sniping is usually doing it from a "safe" position — behind someone's back, through sarcasm, in a low-key way, or indirectly — rather than confronting the person openly and directly. It is criticism that stings but is hard to fully call out, because it is delivered in a sneaky or cowardly way.

"She kept sniping at her colleague's ideas during the meeting instead of offering real feedback."

"He spent the whole dinner sniping at his brother's choices in life."

"The politician's rivals sniped at him on social media rather than debating him face to face."

Notice that in all these examples, the "attacker" is not standing up and making a bold, direct statement. They are taking little shots from a safe distance — that is the essence of sniping in this sense.

If someone does this repeatedly, we might say they are constantly sniping or that they are a sniper (in a figurative sense). It suggests the person is picking at someone, chipping away with small but pointed criticisms, often out of jealousy, resentment, or a desire to undermine without full commitment to open conflict.

A very common modern use: in online auctions (like eBay), to snipe means to place your bid at the very last possible second before the auction closes, so other bidders have no time to outbid you.

"He sniped the auction with just three seconds left and won the item for a low price."

Why is this called sniping? Because, just like a military sniper, you are:

  • Waiting patiently and watching from a distance while others bid.
  • Striking at precisely the right moment — the last second.
  • Giving your target (other bidders) no chance to respond — there is no time left for them to raise their bid.

There is even software called a sniper tool that automatically places a bid in the final seconds of an auction on your behalf. The act itself is called auction sniping.

In informal sports language, especially in hockey, soccer, and basketball, to snipe means to score with a very precise, powerful, impressive shot — hitting exactly the spot you aimed for, leaving the goalkeeper or defender no chance.

"He received the pass and sniped it right into the top corner of the net."

"She sniped a goal from outside the box."

The word is used here with admiration. A player who does this regularly is called a sniper — someone known for clinical, precise finishing. This use keeps the idea of "precise targeting" but drops the negative or covert connotation. It is simply about deadly accuracy.

No matter which context you see it in, the word to snipe always carries these ideas:

  • Precision — not a random attack, but a targeted one.
  • A power imbalance — the sniper has an advantage; the target is vulnerable.
  • Limited ability to respond — the target is caught off guard, with little time or ability to fight back.
  • Often, some element of concealment or patience — the sniper waits for the right moment, or attacks from safety.

When these ideas describe a physical shot, it is literal sniping. When they describe verbal criticism, it is figurative sniping. When they describe an auction tactic, it is strategic sniping. Same word, same soul.

ContextWhat it means
Military / literalShoot at someone from a hidden, distant position
Everyday speechMake petty, pointed criticisms from a "safe" position
Online auctionsBid at the very last second, giving others no time to respond
Sports (slang)Score with a precise, powerful shot

When someone says another person is sniping at them (in conversation), it almost always carries a negative or frustrated tone. It implies the sniping is unfair, cowardly, or annoying — because the sniper won't just say what they mean directly. You would not describe a brave, direct critic as sniping. You reserve that word for someone who takes cheap shots.
14777: A sniper is a highly skilled shooter who fires at targets from a hidden position at a long distance, with extreme precision. The three pillars — concealment, distance, and accuracy — are what separate a sniper from an ordinary shooter.

1. Hidden
A sniper does not stand in the open and shoot. They hide — behind bushes, inside a building, on a rooftop, in a ditch, or camouflaged in tall grass. The target often has no idea where the sniper is, or even that a sniper exists nearby. This secrecy is central to what a sniper does.

2. Far Away
A sniper operates from a great distance — sometimes hundreds of metres, sometimes over a kilometre away. This distance protects the sniper and makes it very difficult for the target to detect or retaliate.

3. Precise
A sniper does not spray bullets randomly. They wait, aim carefully, and fire one precise shot intended to hit a very specific target. The goal is accuracy, not volume of fire. A sniper is trained to account for wind, distance, gravity, and even their own breathing before pulling the trigger.

In warfare and the military
This is the most common and literal use of the word. Militaries around the world train snipers as a specialised role. In a battle or conflict, a sniper might be positioned far from the front line, eliminating high-value targets (such as enemy commanders or machine-gun operators), disrupting enemy movements, or gathering information — all without being seen. Because one skilled sniper can change the course of a battle by targeting key individuals from a distance, they are considered a powerful and feared element of modern warfare.

In law enforcement
Police and counter-terrorism units also use snipers. For example, during a hostage situation, a police sniper may be positioned at a distance, ready to neutralise a threat with a single precise shot if lives are in danger. The objective is the same: accuracy from a hidden, distant location.

• Patience — A sniper may lie still for hours, or even days, waiting for exactly the right moment to act.
  • Discipline — They resist the urge to act prematurely. Timing matters as much as accuracy.
  • Training — Becoming a sniper requires extensive, specialised training in marksmanship, camouflage, map reading, and mental endurance.
  • A sniper rifle — Snipers typically use a long-barrelled rifle with a telescopic sight (scope), which magnifies distant targets and allows for precise aiming. This is very different from the short-range weapons carried by ordinary soldiers.

The word "sniper" is also used outside of warfare to describe a person who attacks, criticises, or undermines others in a sneaky, indirect way — without openly confronting them. Just like a military sniper strikes from hiding, a figurative sniper takes aim at someone from a position of safety or anonymity.

Examples:

  • "He was a political sniper, leaking damaging information about his rivals without ever showing his face."
  • "She faced constant snipers in the media who picked apart every word she said."
  • In online contexts, someone who throws sharp, targeted insults from behind a screen — without engaging in a direct argument — might be called a sniper.

The feeling conveyed is always the same: a hidden attacker making precise, damaging strikes from a distance.
How to Use the Word in Sentences

• "A sniper was positioned on the roof to protect the president during the visit."
  • "The enemy sniper had been hiding in the ruins for three days before anyone noticed."
  • "He wasn't the type to argue openly — he was a sniper, always striking when you least expected it."
  • "The military unit was pinned down by a lone sniper they couldn't locate."

To summarise: a sniper (noun) is someone who shoots with great precision from a concealed and distant position. In its literal sense, it refers to a trained military or law enforcement shooter. In its figurative sense, it describes anyone who makes stealthy, targeted attacks — verbal, political, or otherwise — from a position of safety or anonymity. The word always carries the sense of precision, concealment, and striking from a distance.
14778: A snippet is a small piece of something — specifically, a brief portion that has been taken or pulled out from something larger. The two ideas baked into this word are smallness and origin: a snippet is never the whole thing; it always comes from a bigger source.

Imagine you're reading a long novel. You mark one interesting paragraph and share it with a friend. That paragraph is a snippet — a small extract from the larger whole.

The same logic applies everywhere: a snippet of a song is a few seconds pulled from the full track. A snippet of a conversation is a brief exchange from a longer discussion. A snippet of news is a small piece of information from a larger story.

A snippet is not random or accidental. It's usually deliberately chosen — to share, to preview, or to highlight something worth noticing.

In everyday speech and media, this is the most common use:

  • "I only caught a snippet of what they were saying." (a brief bit of a conversation)
  • "The trailer shows just a snippet of the film." (a short preview clip)
  • "She read us a snippet from her upcoming book." (a small passage)
  • "I heard a snippet of that song and got hooked immediately." (a few seconds of audio)

The word often carries a slight sense of curiosity or incompleteness — you've seen or heard just enough to be intrigued, but not the full picture.

In technology and programming, a code snippet is a small, reusable block of code that performs one specific task. Programmers share snippets on forums, in documentation, or in tutorials. It's not a complete program — it's just the useful little chunk that solves a particular problem. For example, a snippet that shows how to reverse a string in Python.

In search engines, particularly Google, a featured snippet is the highlighted box that appears at the very top of your search results, sometimes even before any links. Google extracts a brief, relevant passage from a webpage — a snippet — and displays it directly so you can get your answer without clicking anywhere.
The tone and feel of the word

"Snippet" is casual and slightly informal in tone. It has a lightness to it. When someone gives you a snippet of information, they're not giving you a lecture or a report — they're giving you a quick taste.

It's also often used with the word "just" or "only" to reinforce how small it is: "I only heard a snippet" or "She shared just a snippet." This signals that the person wishes they had more, or that what was shared was deliberately brief.
How it compares to similar words

• A piece is broad and neutral — it doesn't tell you much about size or origin.
  • A fragment often implies something broken or incomplete, sometimes accidentally.
  • A excerpt is more formal and is almost exclusively used for written text.
  • A snippet sits in a sweet spot: casual, deliberately chosen, brief, and always implying it came from something bigger. It works across text, audio, video, and code — which makes it one of the most versatile words in this family.

• "I only heard a snippet of the conversation, so I don't know the full story."
  • "The artist released a 15-second snippet of her new album online."
  • "He pasted a code snippet into the chat to show us how the function works."
  • "Google showed a snippet from the NHS website right at the top of the results."
  • "The documentary is full of fascinating snippets from old interviews and archival footage."
  • "She gave me a few snippets of gossip but wouldn't tell me everything."

A snippet is a small, deliberately chosen piece taken from something larger — a brief extract that gives you a glimpse or taste without giving you the whole thing. It can apply to conversation, writing, audio, video, search results, or code.
14779: A snit is a state of irritation, agitation, or flustered annoyance — usually over something small or trivial. When someone is in a snit, they are worked up, flustered, and emotionally bothered, but not in a dramatic or deeply serious way. Think of it as the emotional version of a minor storm in a teacup.

Imagine someone planned a small dinner party and one guest showed up 10 minutes late. The host isn't devastated — but they're not fully calm either. They're quietly fuming, a little ruffled, visibly irritated, and perhaps making pointed comments under their breath. That inner state of petty agitation — that flustered, low-grade huff — is a snit.

It sits somewhere between mild annoyance and a small temper tantrum. It is not rage. It is not grief. It is not a full-blown argument. It is that particular uncomfortable emotional state where a person is bothered and perhaps slightly behaving like a child about it.
The key hidden layer: a touch of dismissiveness

This is crucial, and many learners miss it.

When you call someone's reaction a snit, you are gently implying that their upset is a bit disproportionate, petty, or unnecessary — that they're making more of something than it deserves. The word carries a mild, almost affectionate mockery. It subtly says: "You're upset, yes, but let's be honest — it's not that big a deal."

So if you say, "She's in a snit" rather than "She's very upset," you are quietly suggesting that her reaction is a little silly, a little overdone, perhaps even a little childish — without being outright rude about it.

This tone of gentle dismissal is baked into the word itself. It is what separates snit from words like fury or distress, which take the person's emotion fully seriously.

Snit is an informal word, used in everyday conversation. You would say it to a friend, a family member, or in casual writing — not in a formal report or a professional email.

It is used most commonly in American English. If you are speaking British English, people might not use this word as naturally, though they would understand it.

The most common pattern you will encounter is the phrase "in a snit":

"He's been in a snit all morning over that parking ticket."
"Don't get in a snit — it was just a joke."
"She worked herself into a snit because the coffee was cold."

You can also say someone "threw a snit" (meaning they had a small, irritated episode) or simply that they were "in a bit of a snit" (softening it even further).

• "My boss has been in a snit ever since the meeting didn't go his way."
    → He's been visibly irritated, touchy, and difficult to be around — over something relatively minor.
  • "She threw herself into a snit when she wasn't invited to the party."
    → She got worked up and sulky about it, perhaps more than the situation called for.
  • "Oh, ignore him — he's just in a snit because he lost the argument."
    → He's sulking and acting bothered. The speaker thinks it's not a serious reaction.
  • "Why are you in such a snit today? What happened?"
    → You seem flustered and irritable — what's the matter?
How it differs from similar words

FeelingWhat makes snit different

Anger is a broad word that can be serious and intense. A snit is always small-scale — you wouldn't describe someone who just lost a loved one as being "in a snit."

A tantrum is more explosive, more visible, and often associated with children. A snit is quieter and more internal — it's a simmering irritation rather than an outburst.

A huff is very close to a snit. If you're in a huff, you're sulking and offended. A snit is slightly more flustered and agitated, whereas a huff leans more toward sulking and wounded dignity. These two words can often be used interchangeably, though.

Pique (as in "a fit of pique") is similar and slightly more formal. A snit is more colloquial and folksy.
The full picture in one sentence
A snit is an informal word for a small, flustered state of irritation or agitation — with the quiet implication that the person's upset is a bit petty or more than the situation truly warranted.
